stem_md: For which real numbers  $ x>1$  is there a triangle with side lengths  $ x^4\plus{}x^3\plus{}2x^2\plus{}x\plus{}1, 2x^3\plus{}x^2\plus{}2x\plus{}1,$  and  $ x^4\minus{}1$ ?
solution_md:
$ (x^4 \plus{} x^3 \plus{} 2x^2 \plus{} x \plus{} 1) \plus{} (x^4 \minus{} 1) > (2x^3 \plus{} x^2 \plus{} 2x \plus{} 1)\Rightarrow 2x^4 \minus{} x^3 \plus{} x^2 \minus{} x \minus{} 1 > 0$  $ (2x^3 \plus{} x^2 \plus{} 2x \plus{} 1) \plus{} (x^4 \minus{} 1) > (x^4 \plus{} x^3 \plus{} 2x^2 \plus{} x \plus{} 1)\Rightarrow x^3 \minus{} x^2 \plus{} x \minus{} 1 > 0$  $ (2x^3 \plus{} x^2 \plus{} 2x \plus{} 1) \plus{} (x^4 \plus{} x^3 \plus{} 2x^2 \plus{} x \plus{} 1) > (x^4 \minus{} 1)\Rightarrow 3x^3 \plus{} 3x^2 \plus{} 3x \plus{} 3 > 0$ 

These are all true for  $ x > 1$ 

Or, one can realize that  $ x^4\plus{}x^3\plus{}2x^2\plus{}x\plus{}1$  is the largest side, so only the second line is actually necessary.

stem_md:
Are there integers  $ a,b,c,d,x,y,z,t$  such that each of the numbers:
 $ |ay\minus{}bx|,|az\minus{}cx|,|at\minus{}dx|,|bz\minus{}cy|,|bt\minus{}dy|,|ct\minus{}dz|$ 

equals either  $ 1$  or  $ 2005$ ?
solution_md: Suppose the opposite case. Take the sets  $ A\equal{}(a,b,c,d)$  and  $ B\equal{}(x,y,z,t)$ . In each one of this ones, there is at most one even number, otherwise one of the modulus would be even. If all the elements in some set are odd, there would be a even modulus made by two odd elements from the other set. So each set has just one even element. But, in this case, is easy to see that some modulus will be even (you can suppose WLOG that some element of a set is even and divide in some cases), contradiction. It finishes the problem.

stem_md: Find all pairs of positive integers  $ (m,n)$  such that  $ \sqrt{m}\plus{}\frac{2005}{\sqrt{n}}\equal{}2006.$
solution_md:
You're missing  $ (m,n) \equal{} (1605^2,25); (2001^2,401^2); (2005^2,2005^2)$ . 

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>$ \sqrt {m} \plus{} \frac {2005}{\sqrt {n}} \equal{} 2006$   $ \frac {2005}{\sqrt {n}} \equal{} 2006 \minus{} \sqrt {m}$   $ \dfrac{2005^2}{n} \equal{} 2006^2 \plus{} m \minus{} 4012\sqrt {m}$  

Since the left side is rational, the right side must also be rational. Thus,  $ \sqrt {m}$  must be rational. 
Since  $ m$  is an integer, this means that  $ m$  must be a integral perfect square. So let  $ m \equal{} p^2$  for some positive integer  $ p$ . 

Plugging this into the original equation yields:  $ p \plus{} \frac {2005}{\sqrt {n}} \equal{} 2006$ . 

Since  $ p$  and  $ 2006$  are integers,  $ \frac {2005}{\sqrt {n}}$  must also be an integer. Thus,  $ n$  must also be an integer perfect square. So let  $ n \equal{} q^2$  for some positive integer  $ p$ . 

This yields the equation:  $ p \plus{} \dfrac{2005}{q} \equal{} 2006$ . 

Since  $ \dfrac{2005}{q}$  must be an integer,  $ q \mid 2005 \equal{} 5 \cdot 401$ . 

Thus,  $ q \equal{} 1, 5, 401, 2005$ . These yield  $ p \equal{} 1, 1605, 2001, 2005$  respectively. 

Therefore, the solutions are:  $ (m,n) \equal{} (1,1); (1605^2,25); (2001^2,401^2); (2005^2,2005^2)$ .</details>

stem_md: On the plane are given  $ n \ge 3$  points, not all on the same line. For any point  $ M$  on the same plane,  $ f(M)$  is defined to be the sum of the distances from  $ M$  to these  $ n$  points. Suppose that there is a point  $ M_1$  such that  $ f(M_1)\le f(M)$  for any point  $ M$  on the plane. Prove that if a point  $ M_2$  satisfies  $ f(M_1)\equal{}f(M_2),$  then  $ M_1 \equiv M_2.$
solution_md:
Let  $ P_1,P_2,...,P_n$  the points given.

Suppose that  $ M_1 \neq M_2$ . Let  $ M$  be the midpoint of  $ M_1M_2$ .  For all  $ P_i$ , consider the point  $ X_i$  such that  $ P_iM_1X_iM_2$  is a parallelogram. This gives  $ MP_i \equal{} \frac {P_iX}2 \leq \frac {M_1P_i \plus{} M_2P_i}2$ , by triangle inequality, with equality iff  $ P_i$ ,  $ M_1$  and  $ M_2$  are collinear.

Then  $ f(M)\leq\frac{M_1P_1 \plus{} M_2P_2}2\plus{}\frac{M_1P_2\plus{}M_2P_2}2\plus{} ... \plus{}\frac { M_1P_n \plus{} M_2P_n}2$ .

That gives  $ f(M) \leq \frac {f(M_1) \plus{} f(M_2)}2 \equal{} f(M_1) \leq f(M)$ .

Then all the inequalities are equalities, and this implies that all the points given are collinear, absurd.

stem_md:
Let  $ 0 \le \alpha, \beta, \gamma \le \frac{\pi}{2}$  satisfy the conditions
 $ \sin \alpha\plus{}\sin \beta\plus{}\sin \gamma\equal{}1, \sin \alpha \cos 2\alpha\plus{}\sin \beta\cos 2\beta\plus{}\sin \gamma \cos 2\gamma\equal{}\minus{}1.$ 

Find all possible values of  $ \sin^2 \alpha\plus{}\sin^2 \beta\plus{}\sin^2 \gamma$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>For all  $ x \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right]$  we have:  $ \cos 2x \ge \minus{}1$  and  $ \sin x \ge 0$ . 

Thus,  $ \sin x \cos 2x \ge \minus{}\sin x$  with equality iff  $ x \equal{} 0$  OR  $ x \equal{} \dfrac{\pi}{2}$ . 

Therefore,  $ \sin\alpha\cos 2\alpha\plus{}\sin\beta\cos 2\beta\plus{}\sin\gamma\cos 2\gamma \ge \minus{}(\sin\alpha\plus{}\sin\beta\plus{}\sin\gamma) \equal{} \minus{}1$  

with equality iff  $ \alpha,\beta,\gamma \in \left\{ 0 , \dfrac{\pi}{2} \right\}$ . 

Since  $ \sin(0) \equal{} 0$  and  $ \sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \equal{} 1$ , one of  $ \alpha,\beta,\gamma$  must be equal to  $ 1$  and the other two must be equal to  $ 0$ . 

Therefore,  $ \sin^{2}\alpha\plus{}\sin^{2}\beta\plus{}\sin^{2}\gamma \equal{} 1$ .</details>

stem_md: On the plane are marked  $ 2005$  points, no three of which are collinear. A line is drawn through any two of the points. Show that the points can be painted in two colors so that for any two points of the same color the number of the drawn lines separating them is even. (Two points are separated by a line if they lie in different open half-planes determined by the line).
solution_md:
something like this should workFor each drawn line, mark one side with + and the other side with -. Color a point red if it lies on an even number of + regions, otherwise color it blue.
The problem with this approach is that the number of $+$ regions do not vary continuously when one travel along an edge, it may jump more than one, i may even jump an even number. Consider the following example. There are $4$ points, and one is point $P$ lying inside the triangle $ABC$ . For each edge of the triangle, mark the region containing the triangle plus. Then mark the regions divided by $PA$ so that $B$ is plus, $PB$ so that $C$ is plus, and $PC$ so that $A$ is plus. Then each $A,B,C$ will all have two pluses, hence have the same color. But each pair is separated by exactly one line.

For each edge  $ab$  between two points, define a cross along  $ab$  to be a drawn line that separates two endpoints. 

Claim  $1$ : The total number of crosses along all egdes of a triangle is always even. 
Proof: Each line that does not pass through any vertex of the triangle crosses either  $2$  edges or no edge, hence contribute an even number of crosses. Now consider the crosses of lines that pass through exactly one of the vertices. Devide the lines in to  $2002$  group of three lines, such that all lines in same group pass through a point that is not a vertex. Each group contributes either one or three crosses, depending on whether the common point lies inside or outside the triangle. There are an even number of groups, hence the total number of crosses is also even in this case.

Choose a point  $a$  and color red. For any  $b$ , color red if  $ab$  has even number of crosses, blue otherwise. Claim  $1$  ensures that this coloring has the desired property. In fact, we even prove that two points are of same color if and only if their edge has even number of crosses.

stem_md:
The sum of positive real numbers  $ a,b,c$  equals  $ 1$ . Prove that:
 $ \sqrt{\frac{1}{a}\minus{}1}\sqrt{\frac{1}{b}\minus{}1}\plus{}\sqrt{\frac{1}{b}\minus{}1}\sqrt{\frac{1}{c}\minus{}1}\plus{}\sqrt{\frac{1}{c}\minus{}1}\sqrt{\frac{1}{a}\minus{}1} \ge 6.$
solution_md:
let  $ p\equal{}\sqrt{\frac{1}{a}\minus{}1}$  and so on
then since  $ a\plus{}b\plus{}c\equal{}1$  we have  $ p^2q^2\plus{}q^2r^2\plus{}r^2p^2\plus{}2\equal{}p^2q^2r^2$  so let  $ pq\equal{}\frac{1}{\cos A}$  and so on.
it suffices to prove  $ \sum \frac{1}{\cos A} \ge 6$ .

stem_md: In an acute-angled triangle  $ ABC$ ,  $ \omega$  is the circumcircle and  $ O$  its center,  $ \omega _1$  the circumcircle of triangle  $ AOC$ , and  $ OQ$  the diameter of  $ \omega _1$ . Let  $ M$  and  $ N$  be points on the lines  $ AQ$  and  $ AC$  respectively such that the quadrilateral  $ AMBN$  is a parallelogram. Prove that the lines  $ MN$  and  $ BQ$  intersect on  $ \omega _1$ .
solution_md: Let  $ L$  be the midpoint of  $AB$  and  $ P$  the second intersection of  $ \odot (AOC)$  with  $ BQ.$   $ \angle APQ \equal{} \angle BNA \equal{} \angle ABC.$  If  $ R \equiv BQ \cap AC$  and  $D \equiv BN \cap AP,$  then it follows that  $PDNR$  is cyclic. Notice that  $ PQ$  bisects  $ \angle APC,$  since  $ Q$  bisects the arc  $ AC$  of  $\odot(AOC)$   $\Longrightarrow$   $ \angle BPC \equal{} \pi \minus{} \angle ABC \equal{} \angle BNC$   $ \Longrightarrow$   $BPNC$  is cyclic, thus  $ \angle NPR \equal{} \angle ACB.$  But since  $ PDNR$  is cyclic, it follows that  $\angle NPR \equal{} \angle NDR \equal{} \angle ACB \equal{} \angle ABN$    $\Longrightarrow$   $ DR \parallel BA.$  Therefore,  cevian  $NP$  of  $ \triangle BNA$  passes through the midpoint  $ L$  of  $ AB$   $ \Longrightarrow$   $ M$  lies on  $NP$  as desired.

solution_md:
Find all monotone (not necessarily strictly) functions $ f: \mathbb{R}^{ \plus{} }_0\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that: $ f(x \plus{} y) \minus{} f(x) \minus{} f(y) \equal{} f(xy \plus{} 1) \minus{} f(xy) \minus{} f(1) \forall x,y \ge 0$ ; $ f(3) \plus{} 3f(1) \equal{} 3f(2) \plus{} f(0).$
1) Let us solve the easier equation $ (E1)$ : "Find all functions $ g(x)$ from $ \mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ such that : $ g(2x\plus{}y)\minus{}g(2x)\minus{}g(y)\equal{}g(2y\plus{}x)\minus{}g(2y)\minus{}g(x)$ $ \forall x,y\in\mathbb N$ " The set $ \mathbb S$ of solutions is a $ \mathbb R$ -vector space. Setting $ y\equal{}1$ , we get $ g(2x\plus{}1)\equal{}g(2x)\plus{}g(1)\plus{}g(x\plus{}2)\minus{}g(2)\minus{}g(x)$ Setting $ y\equal{}2$ , we get $ g(2x\plus{}2)\equal{}g(2x)\plus{}g(2)\plus{}g(x\plus{}4)\minus{}g(4)\minus{}g(x)$ From these two equations, we see that knowledge of $ g(1),g(2),g(3),g(4)$ and $ g(6)$ gives knowledge of $ g(x)$ $ \forall x\in\mathbb N$ and so dimension of $ \mathbb S$ is at most $ 5$ . But the $ 5$ functions below are independant solutions : $ g_1(x)\equal{}1$ $ g_2(x)\equal{}x$ $ g_3(x)\equal{}x^2$ $ g_4(x)\equal{}1$ if $ x\equal{}0\pmod 2$ and $ g_4(x)\equal{}0$ if $ x\neq 0\pmod 2$ $ g_5(x)\equal{}1$ if $ x\equal{}0\pmod 3$ and $ g_5(x)\equal{}0$ if $ x\neq 0\pmod 3$ And the general solution of $ (E1)$ is $ g(x)\equal{}a\cdot x^2\plus{}b\cdot x\plus{}c\plus{}d\cdot g_4(x)\plus{}e\cdot g_5(x)$ 2) Solutions of the original equation : Let $ P(x,y)$ be the assertion $ f(x\plus{}y)\minus{}f(x)\minus{}f(y)\equal{}f(xy\plus{}1)\minus{}f(xy)\minus{}f(1)$ In a first time, let us forget the monotonous constraint and the equation about $ f(0)$ Comparing $ P(xy,z)$ and $ P(xz,y)$ , we get $ Q(x,y,z)$ : $ f(xy\plus{}z)\minus{}f(xy)\minus{}f(z)\equal{}f(xz\plus{}y)\minus{}f(xz)\minus{}f(y)$ Let then $ p$ a positive integer. $ Q(2,\frac mp,\frac np)$ $ \implies$ $ f(\frac{2m\plus{}n}{p})\minus{}f(\frac{2m}{p})\minus{}f(\frac np)\equal{}f(\frac{2n\plus{}m}{p})\minus{}f(\frac{2n}{p})\minus{}f(\frac mp)$ So $ f(\frac xp)$ is a solution of $ (E1)$ and so $ f(\frac xp)\equal{}a_p\cdot x^2\plus{}b_p\cdot x\plus{}c_p\plus{}d_p\cdot g_4(x)\plus{}e_p\cdot g_5(x)$ $ \forall x\in\mathbb N$ Choosing $ x\equal{}kp$ , it's easy to see that $ a_p\equal{}\frac{a}{p^2}$ , then that $ b_p\equal{}\frac bp$ Choosing $ x\equal{}2kp$ , $ x\equal{}3kp$ and $ x\equal{}6kp$ , it's easy to see that $ c_p\equal{}c$ and $ d_p\equal{}e_p\equal{}0$ And so $ f(\frac xp)\equal{}a(\frac xp)^2\plus{}b(\frac xp)\plus{}c$ $ \forall x,p\in\mathbb N$ And so $ f(x)\equal{}ax^2\plus{}bx\plus{}c$ $ \forall x\in\mathbb Q^{\plus{}*}$ Now, we must remember that $ f(x)$ is monotonous, and so $ f(x)\equal{}ax^2\plus{}bx\plus{}c$ $ \forall x\in\mathbb R^{\plus{}*}$ The condition "monotonous" implies too that $ ab\geq 0$ The condition $ f(0)\equal{}f(3)\plus{}3f(1)\minus{}3f(2)$ implies $ f(0)\equal{}c$ And so the necessary conditions are : $ \boxed{f(x)\equal{}ax^2\plus{}bx\plus{}c}$ $ \forall x\in\mathbb R_0^\plus{}$ with $ ab\geq 0$ And it's immediate to check that these necessary conditions are indeed sufficient.

stem_md: A polygon on a coordinate grid is built of  $ 2005$  dominoes  $ 1 \times 2$ . What is the smallest number of sides of an even length such a polygon can have?
solution_md:
I think you can show a polygon made of unit squares on a checkboard, all side lengths odd, has a different number of black and white squares. Haven't managed to prove it though.
Just for the sake of completeness, since I believe the blog post is no longer there... Suppose the polygon $P$ has all odd sides and let $V$ be the set of its vertices. Color the unit lattice in a chessboard fashion, and for every point $p\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ define $f(p)$ to be the difference between the number of black and white squares (in the chessboard coloring) incident to $p$ . Then $f(p)=0$ for all $p\in\mathbb{Z}^2\setminus V$ , whence \[4B-4W=\sum_{p\in\mathbb{Z}^2}f(p)=\sum_{p\in V}f(p).\]But $P$ has all odd sides, so considering 90 and 270 degree turns separately, we see that $f(p)\in\{-1,1\}$ is constant for all $p\in V$ . In particular, $B\ne W$ . Alternatively, we can use [Green's theorem](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green's_theorem) to get something equivalent---in the notation of the article, $L=-e^{i\pi(x+y)}$ and $M=e^{i\pi(x+y)}$ works. Intuitively, $e^{i\pi t}$ "extends" $(-1)^t$ to non-integer $t$ . See pythag011's Mock USAMO Problem 1 [here](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?f=133&t=458669) for another application of the above ideas. To prove the weaker statement that no domino tiling exists, [height](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/viewtopic.php?p=2554428#p2554428) [functions](http://math.stackexchange.com/questions/36099/transformations-of-domino-tilings/36109#36109) suffice. (For any cycle enclosing a region tiled by dominoes, the sum of the height function over the points/vertices of the cycle must vanish, but if we take the cycle to be the perimeter of $P$ , the odd-side condition makes this impossible. [Conway and Lagarias](http://turgor.allzd.ru/lktg/2009/4/articles/conway.pdf) give a reasonably detailed proof of this in Section 2, Theorem 2.1.)

candidates: We claim the best we can do is two, achievable by putting them all end-to-end in either of the two obvious ways. We prove by induction on the number of dominoes that there will always be at least two sides of even length. For  $ n\equal{}1$ , the result is obvious. Now assume it for  $ n\equal{}k\minus{}1$ . Consider any polygon created by  $ k$  of these dominoes; we claim it has at least two even-length sides. This is because if we remove a domino, the resulting figure will have at least two, and to "get rid" of an even-length side, we would have to position the domino either so that it extended the side or interrupted the middle of the side. In either case, the "exposed" 2-unit side would give another even face - unless one of the existing dominoes covers or adjoins part of it. However, then we would in turn need another domino to cover that domino's exposed side, and in turn another, etc. Hence either the dominoes form a loop, contradicting the definition of a polygon, or there are infinitely many dominoes, which is of course impossible. We therefore have a contradiction, and the minimum is 2, as desired.

This is probably clearer: Every angle of the polygon is  $ 90$  or  $ 270$  and the sum of its angles is  $ 0 \pmod{180}$ . This means the polygon has an even number of sides. It also must have even perimeter; suppose we start at an arbitrary vertex and travel along the whole perimeter. If we travelled  $ u$  units up,  $ d$  units down,  $ l$  units left and  $ r$  units right, then  $ u \equal{} d$ ,  $ l \equal{} r$ , and the perimeter is  $ u \plus{} d \plus{} l \plus{} r \equal{} 2u \plus{} 2l$  which is even. Then the polygon having one side of even length means it has an odd number of sides of odd length and an odd perimeter, which is a contradiction. So at least two sides of even length are needed.

On the other hand, I've only been able to find such regions using an even number of dominoes (actually, a number divisible by 4, I think), and I imagine that non-simply-connected regions probably do not qualify as "polygons," but it does mean that any proof has to exclude this case in some fairly obvious way.  fwolth's proof attempted to do so, but I admit I don't find it incredibly convincing as written. Here's the idea I have been trying to use to tackle this: consider the smallest rectangle of unit squares enclosing the entire polygon. You want to use an algorithm to modify the polygon and "fill" this rectangle, all while keeping careful count of the number of black squares and white squares added. The main thing you can do in this algorithm is something to this effect:
```
XXXX
Xabc
Xdef
Xghi
```

Given two odd sides  $ a \times b$  joined by a 270 degree angle, you can extend them and fill the rectangle they leave out, so you would add all of squares abcdefghi in. This would do two things though: create even sidelengths and change the difference of the black and white squares. One option to fix both is to leave out square i, but I think it's too hard to get the algorithm to terminate, and to fill the rectangle you have to make even sides eventually.

I posted [a conjecture](http://www.artofproblemsolving.com/Forum/weblog_entry.php?t=292336) (mostly empirical) in my blog which shows that the number of 270 degree angles (aka the number of sidelengths) is critical, so having the algorithm target those would seem to be on the right track.

stem_md: In space are marked  $ 2005$  points, no four of which are in the same plane. A plane is drawn through any three points. Show that the points can be painted in two colors so that for any two points of the same color the number of the drawn planes separating them is odd. (Two points are separated by a plane if they lie in different open half-spaces determined by the plane).
solution_md:
This is a nice and quite difficult variant of [APMO 2004/3.](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h82830p474992)

Take a point  $O,$  color it red. Let all points an odd number of planes away from  $O$  be red, and all others blue. This fails only if three points  $A,B,C$  have  $d_{AB}+d_{BC}+d_{CA}$  being even, where  $d$  is the number of planes separating two points. 

A plane only matters in the above sum  $\pmod{2}$  if it separates  $1$  or  $3$  of the pairs  $\{A, B \}; \{B, C\} ;\{C, A\}.$  The latter case is impossible. In the former case, the plane goes through one of  $A,B,$  or  $C$  and separates the other two. **Claim:** Take any two points  $X,Y$  out of the other  $2002$  points that aren't  $A,B,C.$  Then exactly one of the following is true:  $AXY$  separates  $\{B, C\},$   $BXY$  separates  $\{C, A\},$    $CXY$  separates  $\{A, B\}.$ **Proof:** Let  $XY$  intersect plane  $AXY$  at point  $P.$  Then it's easy to see (just draw it out) that no matter where  $P$  lies on the plane, exactly one of the following is true: line  $AP$  intersects segment  $BC$  (equivalent to  $AXY$  separates  $\{B, C\}$ ), line  $BP$  passes through segment  $CA$  (equivalent to  $BXY$  separates  $\{C, A\}$ ), line  $CP$  passes through segment  $AB$  (equivalent to  $CXY$  separates  $\{A, B\}$ ).  $\square$  
There are  $\binom{2002}{2}$  such pairs, an odd number. So  $d_{AB}+d_{BC}+d_{CA}$  is odd, the end.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Find all triples of pairwise distinct positive integers  $(a,b,c)$ , which satisfy the following conditions:  $2a-1$  is divisible by  $b$ ,  $2b-1$  is divisible  $c$  and  $2c-1$  is divisible by  $a$ .

*Proposed by Bohdan Rublyov*
solution_md: Note that  $\left(\dfrac{2a-1}{b}\right)\left(\dfrac{2b-1}{c}\right)\left(\dfrac{2c-1}{a}\right)$  is less than  $\dfrac{2a}{b}\dfrac{2b}{c}\dfrac{2c}{a}=8$ , and is a product of three odd positive integers. Therefore, at least two of these quotients have to be equal to  $1$ . Without loss of generality, let  $\dfrac{2a-1}{b}=\dfrac{2b-1}{c}=1$ . So,  $c=4a-3$ , then  $a|2c-1 \Rightarrow a|8a-7 \Rightarrow a|7$ . If  $a=1$ , we find  $(1,1,1)$ , and  $a=7$  yields  $(7,13,25)$ , as well as its cyclic permutations  $(13,25,7)$  and  $(25,7,13)$ .

stem_md:
In acute-angled triangle  $ABC$ ,  $AH$  is an altitude and  $AM$  is a median. Points  $X$  and  $Y$  on lines  $AB$  and  $AC$  respectively are such that  $AX=XC$  and  $AY=YB$ . Prove that the midpoint of  $XY$  is equidistant from  $H$  and  $M$ .

*Proposed by Danylo Khilko*
solution_md:
Here is an easy complex bash approach. :)
WLOG assume  $(ABC)$  is the unit circle, then we know that   $$ h=\frac{a+b+c-\frac{bc}{a}}{2}, \ m=\frac{b+c}{2}. $$  So, the midpoint of  $HM$ , say  $G$ , is given by  $$ g=\frac{a^2+2ab+2ac-bc}{4a}. $$  For computing  $x$  we know  $x+ab\overline{x}=a+b$  (unit circle chord) and  $\frac{1}{2}(a+c+x-ac\overline{x})=\frac{a+c}{2}$  (because  $AX=XC$  is equivalent to coincidence of the midpoint of  $AC$  and the foot from  $X$  to  $AC$ ). Thus, we find  $$ x=\frac{c(a+b)}{b+c}. $$  Using symmetry,   $$ y=\frac{b(a+c)}{b+c}. $$  Then the midpoint of  $XY$ , say  $F$ , is given by  $$ f=\frac{ac+ab+2bc}{2(b+c)}. $$  We only need to show that the foot from  $F$  to  $BC$  is  $G$ .
However,   $$ \frac{1}{2}(b+c+\frac{ac+ab+2bc}{2(b+c)}-bc\frac{\frac{1}{ac}+\frac{2}{bc}+\frac{1}{ab}}{2(\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c})})=\frac{2a(b+c)+a^2-bc}{4a}=g. $$  And hence we're done!

stem_md: Find all functions  $f:[0,+\infty) \mapsto [0,+\infty)$ , which for all nonnegative  $x,y$  satisfy   $$ f(f(x)+f(y))=xyf(x+y) $$  *Proposed by Igor Voronovich*
solution_md:
Let $P(x, y)$ be the proposition that $f(f(x)+f(y))=xyf(x+y)$ . Let $f(0) = a$ . \begin{align*} P(0, y) :\ & f(a+f(y))=0 P(0, a+f(y)) :\ & f(a+f(a+f(y))) = 0 &\ f(a)= 0 P(a, f(y)) :\ & f^3(y) = af(y)f(a+f(y)) = 0 \end{align*} Substituting $y=0$ into the last statement gives $f^3(0) = 0$ , but $f(a) = f^2(0) = 0$ , hence $f(0)=0$ . \begin{align*} P(0,y) :\ & f(f(y))=0 P(f(x),y) :\ & yf(x)f(f(x)+y) = f(f(f(x))+f(y)) = f(f(y)) = 0 \end{align*} In the last statement, if $y > 0$ , $$ 0 = f(x)f(f(x)+y) $$ In other words, if $f(x) > 0$ , $f(f(x)+y) = 0$ for all nonnegative $y$ . Now consider some $k$ such that $f(k) > 0$ . \begin{align*} P(k, y): f(f(k)+f(y)) &= kyf(k+y) 0 &= kyf(k+y) \end{align*} Which means for any $j > k$ , $f(j) = 0$ . Hence there exists at most $1$ such $k$ . $$ P(k, k): f(2f(k)) = k^2f(2k) = 0 $$ Hence $f(k) \ne \frac k 2$ . Also, since $f(f(k)) = 0$ , $f(k) \ne k$ . Hence either $f(x) = 0$ , or there exists some $k \ne 0$ where $f(k) = c \ne 0, k, \frac k 2$ , and $f(x) = 0$ otherwise. It can be checked that these functions work.
By $P(\dfrac{k}{2}, \dfrac{k}{2})$ we will get that $0 = \dfrac{k^2}{4}f(k)$ so $f(k) = 0$ and this is contradiction with assumption that exists a positive value of $f$ , so its constantly zero.

stem_md:
Two players - Andriy and Olesya play the following game. On a table there is a round cake, which is cut by one of the players into  $2n$  ( $n>1$ ) sectors (pieces), pairwise distinct in weights. Weight of each piece is known to both players. Then they take pieces according to the following rules. At first, Olesya takes  $1$  piece, then Andriy takes  $2$  pieces such that the remaining pieces form a sector. Then they in turns take  $2$  pieces such that after each turn the remaining pieces form a sector. In their last move, one of the players takes one last piece. Each of the players aims to get more of a cake than the opponent. For which  $n$  can Olesya cut the cake such that she wins if in her first move she takes the smallest piece?

*Proposed by Bohdan Rublyov*
solution_md:
I'm not very sure what the poster in #3 is trying to say in the case where  $2 \mid n$ , but something must have gotten wrong there because I think the answer is for all  $n \ne 2, 4$ .

Instead of a cake, we'll deal with a circle of positive reals (representing the weights of the sectors). Note that we can add an arbitrary constant to each real without affecting any strategy considerations, so I'll go ahead and subtract the minimum from each value, so the new minimum is  $0$ . Since  $A$  is forced to start with this piece, we can just consider the game from there on. In effect, we've got a line of  $2n-1$  distinct reals ( $a_1, a_2, ..., a_{2n-1}$ ), and we're taking  $2$  at a time from the ends, except for the last move, in which the last player just takes the remaining number. As before, anyone with strictly greater than half of the total wins.

For  $n$  odd,  $A$  can let  $a_3$  be  $10^N$  for some really large  $N$ , and the other numbers be negligible, like  $1, 2,...$  etc., such that  $a_3$  is strictly greater than half the total. If  $B$  ever takes  $a_1$ ,  $A$  can take  $a_3$  on the next move and win ( $B$  can't take  $a_1$  and  $a_3$  on the same move, and she can't stop  $A$  from taking  $a_3$ ). Hence  $B$  can only take from the right (the end with the higher indices).  $A$  will follow, also just taking the  $2$  rightmost numbers. Due to the parity of  $n$ , it will be  $B$ 's move when only  $a_1, a_2, ..., a_5$  are left.  $A$  will then take  $a_3$  on the next move.

For  $n = 2$ ,  $B$  just takes the two largest numbers. She can take any of the  $3$  possible pairs of numbers, so she can do so.

For  $2 \mid n$ ,  $n \ge 6$ ,  $A$  can let  $a_3 = 10^{N}+2, a_{2n-3} = 10^{N} + 1, a_5 = 10^{N}$  for some big  $N$ , and the rest be around  $1$ . We want  $N$  to be big enough so the other numbers don't matter, so the total is approximately  $3 \cdot 10^{N}$ . Whatever  $B$  takes on her first move ( $(a_1, a_2), (a_1, a_{2n-1}), (a_{2n-1}, a_{2n-2})$ ),  $A$  can either take  $a_3$  and leave the right end with  $a_{2n-1}$  taken, or take  $a_{2n-1}$  and leave the left end with  $a_1$  taken.  $B$  is then forced to take whichever of  $a_3$  and  $a_{2n-3}$  hasn't been taken, else  $A$  will, bringing his total up to  $2 \cdot 10^{N}$ , which is way more than half the total. This leaves the board with  $3$  numbers taken from both ends.  $A$  then takes  $a_5$ , which, again, brings his total up to  $2 \cdot 10^{N}$ .

Finally, for  $n = 4$ , some casebash. Suppose  $A$  has a winning strategy. We call  $(a,b,c)$ , for  $a, b, c \in [1, 7]$ , a *winner* if the sum of  $a_a, a_b, a_c$  is strictly greater than half the total, and a loser otherwise. This means that, regardless of what  $B$  takes,  $A$ 's three numbers must end up being a winner. Also,  $B$  cannot have a winner as a subset of the  $4$  numbers she collects, else clearly  $A$  would have less than half the total. If  $B$  takes  $(1, 2)$ ,  $A$  cannot stop her from taking  $5$  her next turn, so  $(1, 2, 5)$  must be a loser. Similarly,  $(1, 4, 7)$  and  $(3, 6, 7)$  are losers.

If  $B$  starts with  $(1, 2)$ ,  $A$  must respond with  $(3,4)$ , else  $B$  can force him to end with  $(3, 6, 7)$ , a loser. After this,  $B$  can force him to take whichever of  $a_5, a_6, a_7$  is the lowest. Hence,  $(3, 4, 5)$ ,  $(3, 4, 6)$  and  $(3, 4, 7)$  are all winners. By symmetry,  $(1, 4, 5)$ ,  $(2, 4, 5)$  and  $(3, 4, 5)$  are all winners. But then, if  $B$  starts with  $(1, 7)$ ,  $A$  can't stop her from taking either  $(1, 4, 5)$  (which necessitates him taking  $(5, 6)$ ), or  $(3, 4, 7)$  (which necessitates him taking  $(2,3)$ ). Hence  $B$  can always pick up a winner, and thus, well, wins.

The squadron of  $10$  powerful destroyers and  $20$  small boats is about to attack the island. All ships are positioned on the straight line, and are equally spaced. 

Two torpedo boats with  $10$  torpedoes each want to protect the island. However, the first torpedo boat can shoot only  $10$  successive boats, whereas the second one can shoot  $10$  targets which are next by one. Note that they have to shoot at the same moment, so that some targets may be hit by both torpedoes.

What is the biggest number of destroyers that can avoid the torpedoes no matter which targets the torpedo boats choose?

*Proposed by Bohdan Rublyov*
solution_md:
We will prove, that answer is  $3$ .

Give numbers  $1,2,3,...,30$  to ship positions. Divide it to groups  $A_1=(1,2,...,10),A_2=(11,12,...,20),A_3=(21,...,30)$ . If there are more than  $2$   destroyers in  $A$  or in  $C$  then first torpedo boat shoot in this group, and second shoot to others, such that try to hit maximal number of destroyers. 
They both will hit not less than  $x+\lceil \frac{10-x}{2} \rceil \geq 7$ . If there are are less than  $3$  destroyers in  $A$  and  $C$ , then first boat shoot in  $B$ , and second in  $A$  or  $C$  in some destroyer. They will hit not less than  $7$  destroyers.

Set destroyers in  $1,4,7,14,15,16,17,24,27,30$ . Easy to show, that boats cannot hit more than 7.

stem_md:
The sequence  $(x_n)$  is given by  $x_1=a$ ,  $x_{n+1}=\dfrac{1}{2}\left(x_n-\dfrac{1}{x_n}\right)$ . Prove that there is  $a$  such that the sequence  $(x_n)$  has exactly  $2018$  pairwise distinct elements. *(If some element of the sequence is equal to  $0$ , it stops on that element)*

*Proposed by Andriy Hoholev*
solution_md:
Let  $x_{2018}=0,x_{2017}=1$  and we will build sequence as  $x_{n}$  is positive root of  $f(t)=t^2-2x_{n+1}t-1=0$ . This root always exists, because  $f(t)$  always has one negative and one positive root 

We will prove ,that  $x_n>x_{n+1}$  $x_n=x_{n+1}+\sqrt{x_{n+1}^2+1}>2x_{n+1}$ So sequence  $x_1,x_2,...,x_{2018}=0$  is decreasing and has exactly  $2018$  pairwise distinct elements

stem_md:
Given  $N$  positive integers such that the greatest common divisors of all nonempty subsets of them are pairwise distinct. What is the smallest number of prime factors of the product of all  $N$  numbers?

*Proposed by Aleksandr Golovanov*
solution_md:
I assume that we don't care about the  $\gcd$  of an empty set. In this case, the answer is  $N$  for all  $N \ge 2$ , and  $0$  for  $N = 1$  (just pick our number to be  $1$ ).

For  $N \ge 2$ , assume that there is a solution with  $N - 1$  prime factors. Let these be  $p_1, p_2, \ldots p_{N-1}$ . Let our numbers be  $a_1, a_2, \ldots a_n$ . We will now build a set  $S$  as follows:

for each  $i = 1, 2, \ldots N -1$ , we pick any integer  $a_j$  satisfying the following conditions: $a_j$  does not belong to  $S$ . $v_{p_i}(a_j)$  is minimal of those  $a_k$  not belonging to  $S$ .

We add this  $a_j$  to  $S$ .

By the end of this algorithm we have  $|S| = N-1$ . Let the elements of  $S$  be  $s_1, s_2, \ldots$ , and let  $s$  be the number not in  $S$ . Now it is easy to see that  $$ \gcd(s_1, s_2, \ldots s_{N-1}) = \gcd(s_1, s_2, \ldots s_{N-1}, s) $$  contradicting the fact that all the gcds are distinct.

Now we are left with a construction with  $N$  prime factors. This is easy: let  $P$  be the product of the first  $N$  primes, and let  $$ a_i = \frac{P}{p_i} $$  for all  $1 \le i \le N$ , where  $p_i$  is the  $i$ th prime. We can think of each number as a binary string of  $N$  bits, with  $1$  everywhere except in the  $i$ th place. Now the gcd of two or more numbers is just the AND of the strings, which is clearly unique.

In fact if we let the set be  $S$ , we only need that  $gcd(S) \neq gcd(S-{a_i})$  for each i; this guarantees the existence of a prime  $p_i$  such that  $$ v_{p_i} ( a_i ) < v_{p_i} (a_j ) $$  for all  $j \neq i$ . Clearly these  $p_i$  are distinct and we are done.

We claim that the answer is  $N$ .

First, we prove the bound. Assume that there are  $N-1$  primes factors. Let them be  $p_1,p_2,\cdots, p_{N-1}$ .
Let  $a_i=\prod_{j=1}^{N-1} p_j^{x_{i,j}}$  for each  $i$ .
Let  $f(j)=min\{v_{p_j}(a_1),v_{p_j}(a_2),\cdots,v_{p_j}(a_{N-1})\}$  and let  $g(j)$  be the corresponding  $i$  for each  $j$  (that is, if  $f(j)=v_{p_j}(a_i)$  then  $g(j)=i$ , if there are multiple  $i$  satisfying, then take the smallest one.)
Now we see that  $\gcd(a_{g(1)},a_{g(2)},\cdots, a_{g(N-1)})=p_1^{f(1)}p_2^{f(2)}\cdots p_{N-1}^{f(N-1)}=\gcd(a_1,a_2,\cdots,a_N)$ This gives a contradiction, so  $N-1$  prime factors is impossible.

The construction for  $N$  is just  $a_i=\prod_{j\neq i} p_j$ .

Given an acute-angled triangle  $ABC$ ,  $AA_1$  and  $CC_1$  are its angle bisectors,  $I$  is its incenter,  $M$  and  $N$  are the midpoints of  $AI$  and  $CI$ . Points  $K$  and  $L$  in the interior of triangles  $AC_1I$  and  $CA_1I$  respectively are such that  $\angle AKI = \angle CLI = \angle AIC$ ,  $\angle AKM = \angle ICA$ ,  $\angle CLN = \angle IAC$ . Prove that the circumradii of triangles  $KIL$  and  $ABC$  are equal. 

*Proposed by Anton Trygub*
solution_md: Let  $\{A, X\} \equiv \overline{AI} \cap \odot(ABC)$ ,  $\{C, Y\} \equiv \overline{CI} \cap \odot(ABC)$ , and let  $I_A$  be the  $A$ -excenter. Let  $K' \in \overline{AC}$  with  $\overline{XK'} \parallel \overline{CI}$ ; since  $\overline{AIA_1} \sim \overline{AXI_A}$  we know that  $\overline{K'I_A} \parallel \overline{BC}$  and so  $\angle II_AK' = \angle AIC - \angle ACI$ . The inversion at  $I$  fixing  $\odot(ABC)$  then tells us that  $K \in \odot(IXY)$ ; analogously,  $L \in \odot(IXY)$ , and we are done since  $\triangle BXY \simeq \triangle IXY$ .

Let  $ABC$  be an isosceles triangle with  $AB = AC$ . Points  $P$  and  $Q$  inside  $\triangle ABC$  are such that  $\angle BPC = \frac{3}{2} \angle BAC$ ,  $BP = AQ$  and  $AP = CQ$ . Prove that  $AP = PQ$ .

*Proposed by Fedir Yudin*
solution_md: With  $O$  - circumcenter, we have  $ABP\mapsto CAQ$  is a rotation around  $O$ . So with  $ABC$  fixed and  $P$  moving  $PQ/PO$  is fixed. When  $P\in AO$  we see that  $BP$  bisects  $\angle ABO$ . So  $P$  moves on  $B$ -Apollonian circle of  $AO$ . Hence  $AP/PO$  is also fixed. We need to check one case. Take  $P\equiv B$  and Q.E.D.

stem_md:
Let  $ABC$  be a triangle with  $\angle A = 60^\circ$ . Points  $P$  and  $Q$  are chosen on sides  $AB$  and  $AC$ , respectively, such that  $BP = PQ = QC$ . Prove that the circumcircle of  $\triangle APQ$  passes through the projection of the orthocenter of  $ABC$  onto its  $A$ -median.

*Proposed by Fedir Yudin*
solution_md:
Here's my synthetic solution :

WLG, let  $\triangle ABC$  be oriented in the anticlockwise sense.
Let the circumcenter of  $\triangle ABC$  be  $O$ .
Let  $L$  be the point s.t.  $\triangle LBC$  is equilateral and  $L,A$  lie on the same side of  $\overleftrightarrow{BC}$ . Note that  $A,B,C,L$  are concyclic.

Now, we deduce the following :

By  $BP = CQ$ ,  $\triangle LPB, \triangle LQC$  are directly congruent.
So,  $\triangle LPQ,\triangle LBC$  are directly similar  $\implies \triangle LPQ$  is equilateral and is oriented anticlockwise.
By  $BP=PQ=QC$ ;  $LP=PB$  and  $LQ=QC$ .
So,  $\overleftrightarrow{PO},\overleftrightarrow{QO}$  are the perpendicular bisectors of  $\overline{LB},\overline{LC}$  $\implies\measuredangle POQ = 60^{\circ}$ Now, we have  $\measuredangle PAQ = \measuredangle PLQ = \measuredangle POQ = 60^{\circ} \implies A,P,Q,L,O$  are concyclic.
So, we have that  $\odot APQ\equiv\odot AOL$ .

Now, let  $M$  be the midpoint of  $\overline{BC}$ .
Let  $X$  be the  $A\mathrm{-Humpty}$  point of  $\triangle ABC$  i.e. the projection of the orthocenter of  $ABC$  onto the  $A\mathrm{-median}$ . $\therefore MX\cdot MA = MB^2 = MO\cdot ML\implies X,A,O,L$  are concyclic $\implies X$  lies on  $\odot APQ$  (As  $\odot APQ\equiv\odot AOL$ )

Now taking a  $\sqrt{bc}$  inversion+reflection about the  $A$  bisector, the two circumferences are mapped to the lines  $CX^*Q^*$  and  $BX^*P^*$ , with  $X^*\in (ABC)$ . Therefore, by Pascal's theorem on degenerate hexagon  $ABBX^*CC$ , the intersection of the two tangents in  $B$  and  $C$ , called  $T^*$ , is collinear with  $P^*$  and  $Q^*$ . Therefore  $T$  (the inverse of  $T^*$ ) lies on all circumferences  $(APQ)$ . Furthermore, it is well known that this the Humpty point, which lies on the median and on the circumference of diameter  $AH$ .

stem_md:
Andriy and Bogdan take turns putting integers from  $1$  to  $n$  inclusive in the cells of an  $n \times n$  board in such a way that no row or column contains two equal numbers. Andriy begins, and the player who cannot make a move loses. Depending on  $n$ , which player has a winning strategy?


*Proposed by Fedir Yudin*
solution_md: The problem is rather well-known (I mean it's sudoku with a friend ). **Answer.** Bogdan wins for even $n$ and Andriy wins for odd $n$ . **Strategy for even n.** If $n$ is even, it's enough for Bogdan just to play centrally symmetrically. **Strategy for odd n.** In this case it's obvious that Andriy has to "occupy" the central square, let him do so. Then he writes $(n+1)/2$ there and after that if Bogdan writes the number $i$ somewhere, Andriy writes $(n+1-i)$ in the cell symmetric to it.

stem_md:
For any positive integer  $a > 1$ , we define the sequence  $(a_n)$  as follows:  $a_{n+1} = a_n + d(a_n) - 1$ ,  $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ,  $a_1 = a$ , where  $d(b)$  denotes the smallest prime divisor of  $b$ . Prove that for any positive integer  $k$ , the sequence  $d(a_n)$  for  $n \geq k$  is not increasing, i.e. the condition  $d(a_{n+1}) > d(a_n)$  is not true for at least one  $n \geq k$ .

*Proposed by Vadym Koval*
solution_md:
Since  $a_{n+1}$  is uniquely determined by  $a_n$ , it suffices to show for every  $a$  that  $(a_n)$  is not strictly increasing. Suppose the contrary. So, there is some  $a=a_1$  such that  $d(a_{n+1})>d(a_n)$  for all  $n$ . Consider this sequence.
Note that  $d(m)\le\sqrt m$  iff  $m$  is not prime.
If there is  $n$  such that  $a_n=p$  is prime, then  $a_{n+1}=2p-1$  is prime as well (suppose not, then  $d(a_{n+1})\le\sqrt{2p-1}<p=d(a_n)$ , a contradiction). Therefore, by induction,  $a_{n+k}=2^k(p-1)+1$  is a prime number for all  $k\ge0$ . But  $p\mid 2^{p-1}(p-1)+1=a_{n+p-1}>a_n=p$ , so  $a_{n+p-1}$  is not prime. *Contradiction.* Thus,  $a_n$  is never a prime and so  $d(a_n)\le\sqrt{a_n}$  for all  $n\ge1$ . Therefore,  $\sqrt{a_{n+1}}\le\sqrt{a_n+\sqrt{a_n}-1}<\sqrt{a_n}+0.5$ , so  $\sqrt{a_n}<\sqrt{a_1}+0.5(n-1)<0.6n$  for all large enough  $n$  and  $a_{n+1}-a_n=(\sqrt{a_{n+1}}-\sqrt{a_n})(\sqrt{a_{n+1}}+\sqrt{a_n})<0.5\cdot(0.6(n+1)+0.6n)<0.7n$ .
Since  $(d(a_n))$  is a strictly increasing sequence of integers,  $d(a_n)-1>0.9n$  for all large enough  $n$ . But then  $0.9n<d(a_n)-1=a_{n+1}-a_n<0.7n$  for all large enough  $n$ , so contradiction.

stem_md: Show that for any  $n \in N$  the polynomial  $f(x) = (x^2 +x)^{2^n}+1$  is irreducible over  $Z[x]$ .
solution_md:
It follows directly from Lucas's Theorem that  $p \mid \binom{p^n}{k}$  for any positive integers  $n,k$  where  $k = \{1,2,\ldots, p^n-1\}.$  Rewrite 
\begin{align*}
(X^2+X)^{2^{n}}+1&=((X^2+X+1)-1)^{2^{n}}+1 
&= \sum_{k=0}^{2^n} \left(\binom{2^n}{k} (X^2+X+1)^{2n-k}(-1)^k\right)+1 
&=(X^2+X+1)^{2n}+2f(x)+2 
&=(X^2+X+1)^{2n}+2(f(x)+1).
\end{align*}
From Binomial Theorem, terms of  $f(x)$  are of form  $\pm\tbinom{2^n}{k}(X^2+X+1)^k,$  so the entire expression  $f(x)$  is divisible by  $X^2+X+1.$  Since  $X^2+X+1$  is irreducible in  $\mathbb{F}_2[X]$  and  $X^2+X+1$  does not divide  $f(x)+1$  in  $\mathbb{F}_2[X],$  we know by Schönemann's Criterion that  $(X^2+X)^{2^{n}}+1$  is irreducible in  $\mathbb{Z}[X].$

Prove that  $ \angle PMB \equal{}\angle QMC$ .
solution_md:
Denote intersection point of diogonals,intersectıon poınt of angle bısectors  $ \angle B$  and  $ \angle A$  and intersection point of angle bısectors  $ \angle C$  and  $ \angle D$  by  $ L$ ,  $ Y$  and  $ X$ ,respectıvely. $ AD\parallel BC\Rightarrow\angle CXD=\angle AYB=\frac{\pi}{2}$ .
So five points  $ B,L,Y,M$  and  $ A$  are cyclıc. As the same  $ C,L,X,M$  and  $ D$  are also cyclıc.Then $ \angle XMY=\angle XML+\angle YML=\angle XDL+\angle YAL=\angle XCL+\angle YAL=\angle XPY$  $ \Rightarrow X,Y,Q,M,P$  is cyclıc.
It ıs easy to show that  $ XY\parallel AD$ .So $ \angle YPQ=\angle YXQ=\angle QDA\Rightarrow PQDA$  is cyclic.
From all of these $ \angle PMB=\angle PMY-\angle BMY$     $ (1)$  $ \angle QMC=\angle QMX-\angle CMX$     $ (2)$  $ \Rightarrow\angle PMB-\angle QMC=\angle PMY-\angle QMX+\angle CMX-\angle BMY=\angle PMX-\angle QMY+\angle XDC-\angle YAB=\angle PQX-\angle YPQ+\angle XDA-\angle YAD=0$  $ \Rightarrow\angle PMB=\angle QMC$

Point  $ M$  is midpoint of  $ A_{2}B_{2}$ .  $ \angle BCA \equal{} x$ . Find  $ \angle A_{3}MB_{3}$ .
solution_md:
Let  $ H \equiv AA_3A_1 \cap BB_3B_1$  be the triangle orthocenter, let the  $ A_1A_2 \parallel AC,\ B_1B_2 \parallel BC$  meet meet at  $ D \equiv A_1A_2 \cap \B_1B_2,$ , and let these parallels meet the opposite altitudes  $ BB_3B_1,\ AA_3A_1$  at  $ F \equiv A_1A_2 \cap BB_1,\ E \equiv B_1B_2 \cap AA_1.$  The quadrilateral  $ CA_2DB_2$  is a parallelogram with diagonal intersection  $ M \equiv CD \cap A_2B_2.$  The angles  $ \angle A_1EB_1 = \angle A_1FB_1$  are right, the quadrilateral  $ A_1B_1EF$  with the diagonal intersection  $ H \equiv A_1E \cap B_1F$  is cyclic, and  $ HA_1 \cdot HD = HB_1 \cdot HE.$  The altitude feet  $ A_3,\ B_3$  are midpoints of  $ HA_1,\ HB_1 \Longrightarrow$   $ HA_3 \cdot HD = HB_3 \cdot HE$  and the quadrilateral  $ A_3B_3DE$  is also cyclic, let  $ \mathcal M$  be its circumcircle. Let  $ U \in \mathcal M \cap A_1A_2,\ V \in \mathcal M \cap B_1B_2$  be the other ends of diameters spanning the right angles  $ \angle A_1EB_1 \equiv \angle A_3EU = 90^\circ,$   $ \angle A_1FB_1 \equiv \angle B_3FV = 90^\circ.$  The quadrilateral  $ A_3B_3UV$  is a parallelogram, its diagonals cutting each other in half in the center of the circle  $ \mathcal M.$  This parallelogram is inscribed in the parallelogram  $ CA_2DB_2,$  hence they have the same diagonal intersection M, identical with center of the circle  $ \mathcal M.$  The  $ \triangle A_1FH,\ \triangle B_1EH$  are right-angled, the altitude feet  $ A_3,\ B_3$  being midpoints of their hypotenuses  $ HA_1,\ HB_1.$  As a result,
 $ \frac {\angle A_3MB_3}{2} = \angle A_3EB_3 \equiv \angle HEB_3 = 90^\circ - \angle HB_1B_2 =$  $ = 90^\circ - \angle A_1AC = \angle BCA = x$ 
 $ \angle A_3MB_3 = 2x$

stem_md: Find all functions  $f: \mathbb Q \to \mathbb Q$   such that  $ f(x^{2}\plus{}y\plus{}f(xy)) \equal{} 3\plus{}(x\plus{}f(y)\minus{}2)f(x)$  for all  $x,y \in \mathbb Q$ .
solution_md:
Find all functions $ f$ $ Q\to Q$ such that $ f(x^{2} \plus{} y \plus{} f(xy)) \equal{} 3 \plus{} (x \plus{} f(y) \minus{} 2)f(x)$ .
I have a rather complex solution to prove $ f(x)\equal{}x\plus{}1$ : Let $ P(x,y)$ be the property : $ f(x^{2} \plus{} y \plus{} f(xy)) \equal{} 3 \plus{} (x \plus{} f(y) \minus{} 2)f(x)$ Let $ f(0)\equal{}a$ 1) $ P(0,x)$ implies $ f(x\plus{}a)\equal{}af(x)\plus{}3\minus{}2a$ and so : $ \boxed{f(x\plus{}na)\equal{}a^nf(x)\plus{}(3\minus{}2a)(1\plus{}a\plus{}a^2\plus{}\ldots\plus{}a^{n\minus{}1})}$ 2) $ P(x,0)$ and $ P(\minus{}x,0)$ imply $ f(x^2\plus{}a)\equal{}(x\plus{}a\minus{}2)f(x)\plus{}3$ and $ f(x^2\plus{}a)\equal{}(\minus{}x\plus{}a\minus{}2)f(\minus{}x)\plus{}3$ and so : $ \boxed{(x\plus{}a\minus{}2)f(x)\equal{}(\minus{}x\plus{}a\minus{}2)f(\minus{}x)}$ 3) $ P(1,0)$ implies $ f(a\plus{}1)\equal{}(a\minus{}1)f(1)\plus{}3$ but $ 1)$ implies $ f(a\plus{}1)\equal{}af(1)\plus{}3\minus{}2a$ and so $ af(1)\plus{}3\minus{}2a\equal{}(a\minus{}1)f(1)\plus{}3$ and : $ \boxed{f(1)\equal{}2a}$ 4) If $ a\equal{}2$ , then $ 1)$ gives $ f(2n)\equal{}2^n\plus{}1$ and $ 1)\plus{}3)$ gives $ f(2n\plus{}1)\equal{}3\times 2^n\plus{}1$ But then $ P(2,2)$ gives $ f(6\plus{}f(4))\equal{}12$ , so $ f(11)\equal{}12$ but $ f(11)\equal{}f(2\times 5\plus{}1)\equal{}3\times 2^5\plus{}1\equal{}97$ and so $ a\neq 2$ If $ a\equal{}0$ , then $ P(0,0)$ gives $ f(0)\equal{}a\equal{}3$ and so $ a\neq 0$ If $ a\equal{}3$ , then $ 2)$ above with $ x\equal{}1$ gives $ 2f(1)\equal{}0$ but $ 3)$ said $ f(1)\equal{}2a\equal{}6$ and so : $ \boxed{a\notin \{0,2,3\}}$ 5) Using $ x\equal{}a\minus{}2$ in $ 2)$ above, we get $ 2(a\minus{}2)f(a\minus{}2)\equal{}0$ and so, since, from $ 4)$ , $ a\neq 2$ : $ \boxed{f(a\minus{}2)\equal{}0}$ 6) Using $ x\equal{}1$ in $ 2)$ above gives $ f(\minus{}1)\equal{}2a\frac{a\minus{}1}{a\minus{}3}$ (remember with $ 4)$ above that $ a\neq 3$ ). Then $ P(\minus{}1,\minus{}1)$ gives $ f(2a)\equal{}3 \plus{} (2a\frac{a\minus{}1}{a\minus{}3} \minus{} 3)2a\frac{a\minus{}1}{a\minus{}3}$ But $ 1)$ gives $ f(2a)\equal{}a^3\minus{}2a^2\plus{}a\plus{}3$ and so : $ a^3\minus{}2a^2\plus{}a\plus{}3\equal{}3 \plus{} (2a\frac{a\minus{}1}{a\minus{}3} \minus{} 3)2a\frac{a\minus{}1}{a\minus{}3}$ which gives : $ a(a\minus{}1)(a^3\minus{}11a^2\plus{}25a\minus{}27)\equal{} 0$ It's rather easy to see that $ a^3\minus{}11a^2\plus{}25a\minus{}27$ has no rational root and so : $ \boxed{f(0)\equal{}a\equal{}1}$ 7) Then $ 1)$ gives $ f(x\plus{}n)\equal{}f(x)\plus{}n$ and $ f(n)\equal{}n\plus{}1$ Then, Let $ p$ and $ q$ coprimes positive integers. $ P(q,\frac{p}{q})$ gives $ f(q^2\plus{}\frac{p}{q}\plus{}p\plus{}1)\equal{}3 \plus{} (q \plus{} f(\frac{p}{q}) \minus{} 2)(q\plus{}1)$ But $ f(q^2\plus{}\frac{p}{q}\plus{}p\plus{}1)\equal{}q^2\plus{}p\plus{}1\plus{}f(\frac{p}{q})$ (since $ f(x\plus{}n)\equal{}f(x)\plus{}n$ ) and so : $ q^2\plus{}p\plus{}1\plus{}f(\frac{p}{q})\equal{}3 \plus{} (q \plus{} f(\frac{p}{q}) \minus{} 2)(q\plus{}1)$ $ p\plus{}q\equal{}qf(\frac{p}{q}$ and so $ f(\frac{p}{q})\equal{}\frac{p}{q}\plus{}1$ So $ f(x)\equal{}x\plus{}1$ $ \forall x\in\mathbb{Q}^{\plus{}}$ Using $ 2)$ , we have then $ f(\minus{}x)\equal{}\minus{}x\plus{}1$ $ \forall x\in\mathbb{Q}^{\plus{}}$ So $ f(x)\equal{}x\plus{}1$ $ \forall x\in\mathbb{Q}$ And putting back this expression in original equation, we find that this necessary condition is sufficient. And the only solution is $ \boxed{f(x)\equal{}x\plus{}1}$

stem_md: There are 25 people. Every two of them are use some language to speak between. They use only one language even if they both know another one. Among every three of them there is one who speaking with two other on the same language. Prove that there exist one who speaking with 10 other on the same language.
solution_md:
Reformulate the problem:

*Consider a complete graph with  $ 25$  vertices whose edges are colored with several colors such that in any triangle, at least two edges have the same color. Prove that there is a vertex with at least  $ 10$  outgoing edges of the same color.*

Suppose what we have to prove is false.
Call a triple  $ (A,B,C)$  *good* if  $ AB$  and  $ BC$  have the same color.
Count the number  $ N$  of *good* triples  $ (A,B,C)$ . From the condition,  $ N$  is greater or equal to  $ \displaystyle\binom{25}3$ . Consider a vertex  $ X$  and suppose  $ d_1$  of the edges having  $ X$  as an end are of the color  $ 1$ ,  $ d_2$  - color  $ 2$  and so on.
Then  $ d_1\plus{}d_2\plus{}\ldots\plus{}d_c\equal{}24$ . The number of *good* triples  $ (A,B,C)$  with  $ B\equal{}X$  is  $ \displaystyle\sum_{i\equal{}1}^c\binom{d_i}2\equal{}\frac12\left(\minus{}24\plus{}\sum_{i\equal{}1}^cd_i^2\right)$ . We have assumed that  $ d_i\le9$ . If there exist  $ i\neq j$  such that  $ d_i,d_j<9$  then we have  $ d_i^2\plus{}d_j^2\le (d_i\plus{}d_j)^2$  if  $ d_i\plus{}d_j\le9$ , or  $ d_i^2\plus{}d_j^2\le 9^2\plus{}(d_i\plus{}d_j\minus{}9)^2$ , if  $ d_i\plus{}d_j\ge9$ . That's why  $ d_1^2\plus{}d_2^2\plus{}\ldots\plus{}d_c^2\le 9^2\plus{}9^2\plus{}6^2$ , or  $ d_1^2\plus{}\ldots\plus{}d_c^2$  is maximal when  $ c\equal{}3$  and  $ d_1\equal{}d_2\equal{}9$ ,  $ d_3\equal{}6$ . So the number of *good* triples  $ (A,B,C)$  with  $ X\equal{}B$  is at most  $ \displaystyle2\binom92\plus{}\binom62\equal{}87$ . Then  $ N\le25\cdot87$  and from above we have  $ 25\cdot 87\ge N\ge\displaystyle\binom{25}3$ , or  $ 87\ge92$ . Contradiction. So, our assumption that no vertex has at least  $ 10$  outgoing edges of the same color is false.

solution_md:
Construction: Let  $k \equiv 1 \pmod {91}$ . Then set  $n=(2k^2)^4$ . I claim that this works. $n^2+n+1 = (4k^4+2k^2+1)(4k^4-2k^2+1)(4k^4-4k^3+2k^2-2k+1)(4k^4+4k^3+2k^2+2k+1)$   $(4k^4+2k^2+1) \equiv 0 \pmod 7$  and  $(4k^4+4k^3+2k^2+2k+1) \equiv 0 \pmod {13}$ .
This implies that all prime divisors are less than  $\sqrt{n}=4k^4$ , so we are done.  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
Find all primes  $ p$  for that there is an integer  $ n$  such that there are no integers  $ x,y$  with  $ x^3 \plus{} y^3 \equiv n \mod p$  (so not all residues are the sum of two cubes).

E.g. for  $ p \equal{} 7$ , one could set  $ n \equal{} \pm 3$  since  $ x^3,y^3 \equiv 0 , \pm 1 \mod 7$ , thus  $ x^3 \plus{} y^3 \equiv 0 , \pm 1 , \pm 2 \mod 7$  only.
solution_md:
We say that only  $7$  has this property.
Suppose  $p>7$  is a prime of the form  $3k+1$ .
So we have  $k+1$  cubes.
Then if  $x$  can not be written as sum of two cubes then so does  $xt^3$  for every  $t\neq 0$ . (I'm talking in  $\mathbb Z_p$ )
So there are at least  $k$  numbers which can not be written like this.
But by davenport's theorem at least  $(k+1)+(k+1)-1=2k+1$  numbers can be written as sum of two cubes.
But we have  $2k+1+k=3k+1=p$  so in the davenport theorem the equality occurs.
Hence we have all cubes are in the form  $xt$  for some fixed  $t\neq 0$  and all  $a\leq x\leq a+k$ .
But note that cubes are multiplicative so for  $a\leq x,x'\leq a+k$  we have  $a\leq xx't\leq a+k$ .
For  $xt=-1$  we have for all  $a\leq y\leq a+k$   $a\leq -y\leq a+k$  so we have  $a=-\frac k2$ .
For  $x=1$  we have  $-\frac k2\leq t\leq \frac k2$ . Now because  $p>7$  we have  $-\frac k2\leq 2\leq \frac k2$ .
Now take  $x=2$  and move  $x'$  from  $1$  to  $\frac k2$  so once  $xx't$  will not be in  $[-\frac k2,\frac k2]$  some time and we are done.

stem_md: There is a row that consists of digits from  $ 0$  to  $ 9$  and Ukrainian letters (there are  $ 33$  of them) with following properties: there aren’t two distinct digits or letters  $ a_i$ ,  $ a_j$  such that  $ a_i > a_j$  and  $ i < j$  (if  $ a_i$ ,  $ a_j$  are letters  $ a_i > a_j$  means that  $ a_i$  has greater then  $ a_j$  position in alphabet) and there aren’t two equal consecutive symbols or two equal symbols having exactly one symbol between them. Find the greatest possible number of symbols in such row.
solution_md:
Yes, the answer is 73.
I prove it as follows:

Consider some sequence (not necessarily of maximal length). When looking just at its digits (or at its letters), we obtain non-decreasing sequences.

Let  $b_i$  be the number of occurrences of the digit  $i$  in the sequence, as well as  $c_{i,j}$  the number of letters written between the occurrences  $j$  and  $j+1$  of the letter  $i$ , for  $j < b_i$ . W.l.o.g., we can suppose that  $b_i \geq 1$ , and we must have  $c_{i,j} \geq 2$ . Moreover, let  $c_{-\infty}$  be the number of letters written before the first occurrence of  $0$ , and  $c_\infty$  the number of letters written after the last occurrence of  $9$ . We get  $32 \geq c_{-\infty} + \sum_{i=0}^9 (-1+\sum_{j=1}^{b_i-1}c_{i,j}) + c_{\infty}$ , i.e.  $42 \geq c_{-\infty} + \sum_{i=0}^9 \sum_{j=1}^{b_i-1}c_{i,j} + c_{\infty}$ , and the sequence has a length  $L = c_{-\infty} + \sum_{i=0}^9 (b_i + \sum_{j=1}^{b_i-1}c_{i,j}) + c_\infty \leq 42 + \sum_{i=0}^9 b_i$ . Moreover,  $42 \geq c_{-\infty} + \sum_{i=0}^9 \sum_{j=1}^{b_i-1}c_{i,j} + c_{\infty} \geq 0 + \sum_{i=0}^9 \sum_{j=1}^{b_i-1}2 + 0 = 2 \sum_{i=0}^9 b_i - 20$ , and therefore  $ \sum_{i=0}^9 b_i \leq \frac{42+20}{2} = 31$ , so that  $L \leq 42 + 31 = 73$ .

Conversely, the sequence 0АБ01БВ12ВГ23ГҐ34ҐД45ДЕ56ЕЄ67ЄЖ78ЖЗ89ЗИ9ІЇ9ЙК9ЛМ9НО9ПР9СТ9УФ9ХЦ9ЧШ9ЩЬ9ЮЯ9 is of length 73. (Of course, I used equality cases in the above inequalities to find such an example)

stem_md: Two circles  $ \omega_1$  and  $ \omega_2$  tangents internally in point  $ P$ . On their common tangent points  $ A$ ,  $ B$  are chosen such that  $ P$  lies between  $ A$  and  $ B$ . Let  $ C$  and  $ D$  be the intersection points of tangent from  $ A$  to  $ \omega_1$ , tangent from  $ B$  to  $ \omega_2$  and tangent from  $ A$  to  $ \omega_2$ , tangent from  $ B$  to  $ \omega_1$ , respectively. Prove that  $ CA \plus{} CB \equal{} DA \plus{} DB$ .
solution_md:
Let  $ a_1, b_1$  be tangents of  $ \omega_1$  from  $ A, B$  other than  $ AB$  and let  $ a_2, b_2$  be tangents of  $ \omega_2$  from  $ A, B$  other than  $ AB.$  Then  $ C \equiv a_1 \cap b_2$  and  $ D \equiv a_2 \cap b_1.$  Let the tangent of  $ \omega_1$  from  $ A, B$  meet at  $ E \equiv a_1 \cap b_1$  and let the tangents of  $ \omega_2$  from  $ A, B$  meet at  $ F \equiv a_2 \cap b_2.$  Let  $ A_1, B_1$  be tangency points of  $ a_1, b_1$  with  $ \omega_1$  and let  $ A_2, B_2$  be tangency points of  $ a_2, b_2$  with  $ \omega_2.$  
 $ AE \plus{} BF \equal{} (AA_1 \plus{} A_1E) \plus{} (BB_2 \plus{} B_2F) \equal{} AP \plus{} B_1E \plus{} BP \plus{} A_2F \equal{}$   $ \equal{} AA_2 \plus{} B_1E \plus{} BB_1 \plus{} A_2F \equal{} (AA_2 \plus{} A_2F) \plus{} (BB_1 \plus{} B_1E) \equal{} AF \plus{} BE$ 
 $ \Longrightarrow$  concave  $ AEBF$  is tangential with an incircle  $ \Longrightarrow$  convex  $ CEDF$  is tangential with the same incircle  $ \Longrightarrow$ 
 $ CE \plus{} FD \equal{} FC \plus{} DE,\ CE \minus{} FC \equal{} DE \minus{} FD$ 

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>This is a special case of general theorem at [http://www.mathlinks.ro/viewtopic.php?t=247411](http://www.mathlinks.ro/viewtopic.php?t=247411). In this special case, two directed circles are of zero radius - the points  $ A, B.$  The other two circles  $ \omega_1, \omega_2$  are directed in the opposite directions; as directed circles, they are not tangent at all. Since the common directed tangents  $ \overline{AP}$  of  $ A, \omega_1$ ;  $ \overline{PB}$  of  $ \omega_1, B$ ;  $ \overline{BP}$  of  $ B, \omega_2$ ; and  $ \overline{PA}$  of  $ \omega_2, A$  touch the point  $ P$  - a circle of zero radius - the other common directed tangents  $ \overline{EA}, \overline{BE}, \overline{FB},$  and  $ \overline{AF}$  of these circle pairs also touch a single directed circle.</details>
WLOG, let  $ \omega_1 < \omega_2.$ 
 $ CA \plus{} CB \equal{} (FA \minus{} FC) \plus{} (CE \plus{} EB) \equal{} (FA \plus{} EB) \plus{} (CE \minus{} FC) \equal{}$  $ \equal{} (EA \plus{} FB) \plus{} (DE \minus{} FD) \equal{} (DE \plus{} EA) \plus{} (FB \minus{} FD) \equal{} DA \plus{} DB.$

stem_md: Prove that there exist infinitely many pairs  $ (a, b)$  of natural numbers not equal to  $ 1$  such that  $ b^b \plus{}a$  is divisible by  $ a^a \plus{}b$ .
solution_md: I suppose that  $ a \neq b$ . Take an arbitrary even number  $ a$  and  $ b\equal{}a^{a\plus{}2} \minus{} a^{a} \plus{} a$ . Then  $ a^a \plus{} b \equal{} a^{a\plus{}2} \plus{} a$  and  $ b^b \plus{} a \equiv (\minus{}a^a)^{b} \plus{} a \equiv a^{ab} \plus{} a \pmod{a^a\plus{}b}$  since  $ b$  is even as  $ a$  is even. So we have to prove that  $ a^{a\plus{}1} \plus{} 1 | a^{ab\minus{}1} \plus{} 1$ . Since  $ a\plus{}1$  is odd it sufficies to show that  $ a\plus{}1|ab\minus{}1$ . But this is clear as  $ ab \minus{} 1 \equal{} a^{a\plus{}3} \minus{} a^{a\plus{}1} \plus{} a^2 \minus{} 1 \equal{} (a\minus{}1)(a\plus{}1)(a^{a\plus{}1} \plus{} 1)$ .

stem_md: There is graph  $ G_0$  on vertices  $ A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$ . Graph  $ G_{n \plus{} 1}$  on vertices  $ A_1, A_2, \ldots, A_n$  is constructed by the rule:  $ A_i$  and  $ A_j$  are joined only if in graph  $ G_n$  there is a vertices  $ A_k\neq A_i, A_j$  such that  $ A_k$  is joined with both  $ A_i$  and  $ A_j$ . Prove that the sequence  $ \{G_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$  is periodic after some term with period  $ T \le 2^n$ .
solution_md:
I don't have much time to type this up, but here is a somewhat detailed sketch (hopefully correct):

<details><summary>Click to expand</summary>We prove via induction; the base cases n=1,2,3 are trivial. Assume that a complete subgraph  $ K_i$ ,  $ i\ge 3$ , exists at some stage  $ G_k$ . Then this particular subgraph must also exist at any subsequent stage. Hence, the size of the largest subgraph at any stage is monotonically increasing. Since  $ i\le n$ , at some point this largest size will become constant; assume this size is  $ i_0$ . Then no member of this  $ K_{i_0}$  can be connected to any member outside of it, since otherwise at the next stage we will have a  $ K_{i_0\plus{}1}$ , contradicting the fact that  $ i_0$  is constant. Therefore, we can split the set of  $ n$  members into two groups:  $ K_{i_0}$  and everyone not in  $ K_{i_0}$  and apply the induction hypothesis. Therefore, the period of these n vertices is at most  $ 2^{|K_{i_0}|}\times 2^{n\minus{}|K_{i_0}|}\equal{}2^n$ , as desired. 

Now suppose that no such such subgraph will ever exist. Then at any stage, there must be at most  $ n$  segments because otherwise by the Pigeonhole principle, some vertex will have at least three segments coming out of it, at which point the next stage will have a complete  $ K_i$ ,  $ i\ge 3$ . Then consider the number of segments that exist at any stage  $ G_k$  (basic counting argument). It is not hard to see that this value never increases, so at some point it becomes constant. For this point, any vertex with edges coming out of it has exactly 2 such edges; therefore, we can decompose the set of  $ n$  vertices into disjoint cycles. If there are at least two cycles, we can apply the induction hypothesis. If there is exactly one, then we have two cases, whether this cycle length is even or odd. If it is even, at the next stage it will decompose into two cycles, so we are done. If it is odd, assume it has size  $ r$ . If  $ r<n$ , then we can again use the induction hypothesis. So  $ r\equal{}n$ ; then basic number theory guarantees that this cycle has period at most  $ \phi(n)$ , which is clearly less than  $ 2^n$ , as desired.</details>

stem_md: Let  $ ABCDE$  be convex pentagon such that  $ S(ABC) \equal{} S(BCD) \equal{} S(CDE) \equal{} S(DEA) \equal{} S(EAB)$ . Prove that there is a point  $ M$  inside pentagon such that  $ S(MAB) \equal{} S(MBC) \equal{} S(MCD) \equal{} S(MDE) \equal{} S(MEA)$ .
solution_md:
Note the following Lemma:  If in quadrilateral  $ XYZT$    $ S(XYT)\equal{}S(XZT)$ , than  $ YZ\parallel{}XT$ . 
Proof: Denote by  $ a,b$  the distances from points  $ Y,Z$  to  $ XT$  (Respectively). Than,   $ a\equal{}\frac{2S(XYT)}{XT}\equal{}\frac{2S(XZT)}{XT}\equal{}b$ , which means  $ a\equal{}b$  and hence,  $ YZ\parallel{}XT$ . This way the Lemma is proved. 
    Apply the Lemma to  $ ABCD$ , where by the condition,  $ S(ABC)\equal{}S(BCD)$ . So,  $ AD\parallel{}BC$ . Analogeously,  $ BE\parallel{}CD$ ,  $ AC\parallel{}DE$ ,  $ DB\parallel{}EC$  and  $ EC\parallel{}AB$ .  Denote  $ K\equal{}AC,BE$ ,  $ L\equal{}BD,AC$ ,  $ Q\equal{}CE,BD$ ,  $ N\equal{}AD,CE$ ,  $ P\equal{}AD,BE$ .  (Here by  $ U\equal{}XY,ZT$  we mean that  $ U$  is the intersection point of  $ XY$  and  $ ZT$ ). 
   Denote  $ M\equal{}AQ,KD$ . We will prove that  $ M$  also lies on lines  $ EL,BN,CP$ .  
   Note that  $ ABQE$  and  $ ABCN$  are parallelograms. So, $ QE\equal{}CN$  and  $ CQ\equal{}EN$ . Analogeously,  $ EP\equal{}KB$ , $ EN\equal{}QC$  and  $ AP\equal{}ED$ . As  $ PN\parallel{}AD\parallel{}BC$ ,  $ \frac{EP}{EB}\equal{}\frac{EN}{EC}$ , which means  $ \frac{KB}{EB}\equal{}\frac{QC}{EC}$ , which imply  $ KQ\parallel{}AD$ . In trapezoid  $ AKQD$   $ L\equal{}AK,DQ$  and  $ M\equal{}AQ,KD$ . So, by the well-know fact,  $ LM$  passes through the midpoints of  $ KQ$  and  $ AD$ . Call this line  $ l$ . On the other hand,  $ KPNQ$  is also trapezoid where  $ E\equal{}KP,QN$ . So, line joining the midpoints of  $ PN$  and  $ KQ$ , passes through  $ E$ , but as we've already mentioned,  $ AP\equal{}ND$ , which imply that the midpoints of  $ PN$  and  $ AD$  coincide each other and therefore,  $ l$  passes through  $ E$ . So,  $ M$  lies on  $ EL$ . The same way we can prove that  $ M$  lies on  $ BN$  and  $ CP$ . 
    Now call the midpoint of  $ AC$   $ T$ . Then,  $ S(ABT)\equal{}S(CBT)$  and  $ S(AMT)\equal{}S(CMT)$  (As  $ BT$  is median in triangles  $ ABC$  and  $ AMC$ ). So,  $ S(AMB)\equal{}S(ABT)\plus{}S(AMT)\equal{}S(CBT)\plus{}S(CMT)\equal{}S(BMC)$ . Analogeously,  $ S(BMC)\equal{}S(CMD)$ ,  $ S(CMD)\equal{}S(DME)$ , $ S(DME)\equal{}S(MEA)$  and  $ S(MEA)\equal{}S(MAB)$ . 
    Finally,  $ S(MBC)\equal{}S(MCD)\equal{}S(MDE)\equal{}S(MEA)\equal{}S(MAB)$  and there exists such an  $ M$ , as desired.  Lasha Lakirbaia :)

stem_md: Prove that for all natural  $ m$ ,  $ n$  polynomial  $ \sum_{i \equal{} 0}^{m}\binom{n\plus{}i}{n}\cdot x^i$  has at most one real root.
solution_md:
It is easy to see these polynomials have no positive roots.
Now we assume  $ x<0$  and denote the polynomial as  $ P(n,m)$ . $ (x-1)P(n,m)=\sum_{i=1}^{m+1}\binom{n+i-1}n x^i-\sum_{i=0}^m\binom{n+i}n x^i
=\binom{n+m}m x^{m+1}-\sum_{i=0}^m\binom{n+i-1}{n-1}x^i
=\binom{n+m}m x^{m+1}-P(n-1,m)$ 

or
 $ P(n,m)-\frac1{1-x}P(n-1,m)=-\binom{n+m}nx^{m+1}\frac1{1-x}$ .

Then we can prove by induction $ P(n,m)=\frac1{(1-x)^n}P(0,m)-\sum_{i=1}^n\binom{m+i}ix^{m+1}\frac1{(1-x)^{n+1-i}}$ 

or
 $ P(n,m)=\frac1{(1-x)^n}+\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{m+i}i(-x^{m+1})\frac1{(1-x)^{n+1-i}}$ 

When  $ m$  is even, we see each term on RHS is positive. So  $ P(n,m)$  has no real root for even  $ m$ .
Also  $ P(n,m)>0,\forall 2|m$ .

We notice that $ P^'(n,m)=\sum_{i=1}^m\binom{n+i}n ix^{i-1}
=(n+1)\sum_{i=1}^m\binom{n+i}{n+1} x^{i-1}
=(n+1)\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\binom{n+1+i}{n+1}ix^i
=(n+1)P(n+1,m-1)$ .

If  $ m$  is odd, we see  $ P^'(n,m)>0$  implies  $ P(n,m)$  is monotone, then  $ P(n,m)$  has exactly one real root.

Q.E.D.

solution_md: So, we use complex numbers .Say,  $\arg w = 60^{\circ} $  so  $w^2-w+1=0$ . WLOG assume that  $(O)$  is unit circle and  $a=1$ .  $\implies e=w^2=c\cdot w$  and  $d=b\cdot w$ . stem_md: Two circles  $\gamma_1, \gamma_2$  are given, with centers at points  $O_1, O_2$  respectively. Select a point  $K$  on circle   $\gamma_2$  and construct two circles,  one  $\gamma_3$  that touches circle  $\gamma_2$  at   point  $K$  and circle  $\gamma_1$  at a point  $A$ , and the other  $\gamma_4$  that touches circle  $\gamma_2$  at point  $K$  and circle  $\gamma_1$  at a point  $B$ . Prove that, regardless of the choice of  point K on circle  $\gamma_2$ , all lines  $AB$  pass through a fixed point of the plane.
solution_md: WLOG assume that  $\gamma_3$  and  $\gamma_1$  touch externally, then  $\gamma_4$  and  $\gamma_1$  touch internally. Denote by  $O_3$  and  $O_4$  centers of  $\gamma_3$  and  $\gamma_4$ . Note that triples  $(O_4,O_1,B), (O_1,A,O_3), (O_3,K,O_4)$  are collinear. Also,  $O_4B=O_4K, O_1B=O_1A, O_3A=O_3K$ , so  $(ABK)$  is  $O_4$ -excircle of  $\triangle O_4O_1O_3$ . Let  $(ABK)$  intersect  $O_1O_2$  at  $X,Y$ , then  $R_{\gamma_2}^2=O_2X\cdot O_2Y$  and  $R_{\gamma_1}^2=O_1X\cdot O_1Y$ , so  $(X,Y)$  is a pair of inverse points for two different inversions on line  $O_1O_2$  (independent from  $K$ ), hence the are fixed. Finally, let  $\gamma_1$  intersect  $O_1O_2$  at  $P,Q$ , then since  $AB$  is radical axis of  $\gamma_1$  and  $(ABK)$ ,  $AB$  intersects  $O_1O_2$  at center of inversion, defined by pairs  $(P,Q)$  and  $(X,Y)$ , so we are done.

Let  $S$  be a set consisting of  $n$  elements,  $F$  a set of subsets of  $S$  consisting of  $2^{n-1}$  subsets such that every three such subsets have a non-empty intersection.
a) Show that the intersection of all subsets of  $F$  is not empty.
b) If you replace the number of sets from   $2^{n-1}$  with   $2^{n-1}-1$ , will the previous answer change?
solution_md:
a)Let  $S=\{1,2,...,n\}$ .For any subset  $A$  of  $S$  pair it with  $A^c$ .So there are exactly  $2^{n-1}$  tuple of the form  $(A,A^c)$ .At most one element from a tuple can be in  $F$  because otherwise there will 2 non intersecting element in  $F$ .So at most  $2^{n-1}$  sets can be in  $F$ .On the other hand given that  $|F|=2^{n-1}$ .So for each subset  $A$  of  $S$  exactly one of  $A$  or  $A^c$  will be in  $F$ .

Claim:  $F$  be a family of  $2^{n-1}$  subsets of  $\{1,2,...,n\}$  with the property that any 2 sets intersects in some points.Then there are 2 sets  $A$  and  $B$  in  $F$  which intersects in exactly one point.

proof:Consider  $\{1\}\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \  \ \ \{2,3,...,n\}$  $\{1,2\}\ \ \ \ \  \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \{3,4,...,n\}$  $\{1,2,3\}\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \{4,5,...,n\}$  $.....$  $\{1,2,...n-1\}\ \ \ \ \ \{n\}$ note that from each row exactly one set will be in  $F$ .So If  $\{1\}$  ,  $\{1,2\}$  are in  $F$  we are done.If  $\{1,2\}$ , $\{2,3,...n\}$  are in  $F$  we are done.Otherwise,  $\{1,2\}$   $\{2,3,...n\}$  are in  $F$ .Now if the second column set from a row and the first column set from the next row are in  $F$  we are done.Otherwise, we have all the second column sets in  $F$ .But then  $\{2,3,...,n\}$  and  $\{n\}$  are in  $F$  which intersect in one element. $\blacksquare$ Now as every 3 elements intersects in some point and there are 2 set intersects in one point so all the sets intersect in a common point.

stem_md: Find all odd prime numbers  $p$  for which there exists a natural number  $g$  for which the sets \[A=\left\{ \left( {{k}^{2}}+1 \right)\,\bmod p|\,k=1,2,\ldots ,\frac{p-1}{2} \right\}\] and \[B=\left\{ {{g}^{k}}\bmod \,p|\,k=1,2,...,\frac{p-1}{2} \right\}\] are equal.
solution_md:
I think the answer is that there is no such  $p$  besides  $p=3$ . 

First, I redefined the sets such that \[A'=\left\{ \left( {{k}^{2}} \right)\,\bmod p|\,k=1,2,\ldots ,\frac{p-1}{2} \right\}\] and \[B'=\left\{ {{g}^{k}}-1 \bmod \,p|\,k=1,2,...,\frac{p-1}{2} \right\}\] are equal.

Clearly,  $g$  has to be a generator  $\pmod{p}$ . Given this,  $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$  because otherwise, there exists some  $k$  such that  $k^2 + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ . Therefore, we may say that there is no two elements in  $A'$  add up to be  $\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$ , and we let  $p = 4n+3$ . 

Now essentially, we need that each element in  $A'$ , that is  $g^2, g^4, .... g^{4n+2}$ , to map 1:1 via  $\pmod{p}$  to the elements of  $B'$ , that is  $g-1, g^2-1, ... g^{2n+1}-1$ . Consequently, we have that  $g, g^3, ... , g^{4n+1}, 0$   map 1:1 to  $g^{2n+2}-1, g^{2n+3}-1, ..., g^{4n+2}-1, -1$ . Let  $g -1 \equiv g^{2m} \pmod{p}$  for  $m \leq 2n+1$ . Then, multiplying  $g^{4n-1}$  to each side, we have that  $1-g^{4n-1} \equiv g^{2m-1} \pmod{p}$ . In other words,  $g^{4n-1}-1$  is equivalent to  $-g^{2m-1}$  in  $\pmod{p}$ . As  $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$ , we know that  $-g^{2m-1} \equiv g^{2\ell} \pmod{p}$ . In other words,  $g, g^3, ... , g^{4n+1}, 0$   doesn't map 1:1 to  $g^{2n+2}-1, g^{2n+3}-1, ..., g^{4n+2}-1, -1$ . Contradiction.

stem_md: Find all pairs of odd integers  $a$  and  $b$  for which there exists a natural number $ c$  such that  the number  $\frac{c^n+1}{2^na+b}$  is integer for all natural  $n$ .
solution_md:
If  $a=b=1$ , then  $c=2$  works. We show that neither of  $a>1$  or  $b>1$  is possible.

Take firstly  $n = 2^t$  for any positive integer  $t$ . Let  $p$  be a prime divisor of  $2^{2^t}a+b$  - then  $p\geq 3$  as  $a,b$  are odd by the problem statement. From  $c^{2^t} \equiv -1 \pmod p$  we get  $c^{2^{t+1}} \equiv 1 \pmod p$  and  $c^{2^k} \not\equiv 1 \pmod p$  for  $k \leq t$  (else do repeated squaring to reach  $c^{2^t} \equiv 1 \pmod p$ , contradiction for  $p\geq 3$ ), which implies that the order of  $c$  mod  $p$  equals  $2^{t+1}$ . In particular,  $p\equiv 1 \pmod {2^{t+1}}$ , so all prime factors of  $2^{2^t}a+b$  are  $1$  mod  $2^{t+1}$ . Hence, by multiplying all prime factors with their multiplicities, we get  $b\equiv 2^{2^t}a+b \equiv 1 \pmod{2^{t+1}}$ . Since  $t$  is arbitrary, we must have  $b=1$ .

Now consider  $n=p$  to be a prime, so  $2^pa + 1$  divides  $c^p + 1$ . Let  $q \geq 3$  be a prime factor of  $2^pa + 1$  - then it also divides  $c^p + 1$ . Hence  $c^{2p} \equiv 1 \pmod q$ , but  $c, c^p \not\equiv 1 \pmod q$ , so the order of  $c$  mod  $q$  is  $2$  or  $2q$ . Therefore  $q$  divides  $c+1$  or  $p$  divides  $q-1$ . Hence  $2^pa + 1 = A_pB_p$ , where  $A_p \equiv 1 \pmod p$  is a product of primes  $1$  mod  $q$  and  $B_p$  is a product of prime divisors (possibly with multiplicities) of  $c+1$ . Fortunately,  $\nu_q(B_p) \leq \nu_q(2^pa + 1) \leq \nu_q(c^p + 1) = \nu_q(c+1)$  for  $q\neq p$  by Lifting the Exponent Lemma, so  $B_p \leq c+1$  if  $p>c+1$  (so that  $q\neq p$  in the last line always holds). Now taking  $p > 2a+1, p > c + 1$  and using  $2a+1 \equiv 2^pa + 1 \pmod p$  by Fermat's Little Theorem forces  $2a + 1 \equiv B_p \pmod p$ , and thus  $B_p = 2a+1$ .

Since  $B_p$  divides  $2^pa + 1$ , we deduce that  $2a+1$  divides  $2^pa + 1$  for all sufficiently large primes  $p$ . However, now by taking  $p\equiv -1 \pmod {\varphi(2a+1)}$  (possible by Dirichlet's theorem), we get by Euler's theorem that  $0 \equiv 2^{p+1}a + 2 \equiv a+2 \pmod {2a+1}$ , which requires  $2a+1 \leq a+2$ , hence  $a=1$ , as desired.

<details><summary>Remark on alternative approach</summary>By considering  $n=p-1$ , where  $p$  is a prime divisor of  $a+1$ , it follows that  $a+1$  must be a power of  $2$ . However, I cannot see a direct argument to take care of this case.</details>

stem_md: For the nonnegative numbers  $a, b, c$  prove the inequality:  $$ \frac{a}{b+c}+\frac{b}{c+a}+\frac{c}{a+b}+\sqrt{\frac{ab+bc+ca}{a^2+b^2+c^2}}\ge \frac52 $$
solution_md:
Cool problem.
Firstly by Cauchy-Schwarz we have  $$ (\sum_{cyc}\frac{a}{b + c}) (\sum_{cyc}a(b+c)\geq (\sum_{cyc}a)^2 $$  From there we have   $$ \sum_{cyc}\frac{a}{b + c}\geq \frac{\sum_{cyc} a^2 + 2\sum_{cyc}ab}{2\sum_{cyc}ab} $$  Now let's denote  $M = \sum_{cyc}a^2$ ,  $N = \sum_{cyc}ab$ .
Then let's watch our starting inequality   $$ \sum_{cyc}\frac{a}{b + c} + \sqrt{\frac{N}{M}} \geq \frac{M}{2N} + 1 + \sqrt{\frac{N}{M}} $$  . Now by using  $AM-GM$  on  $(\frac{M}{2N}, \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{N}{M}}, \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{N}{M}})$  we get that   $$ \frac{M}{2N} + 1 + \sqrt{\frac{N}{M}} \geq (\frac{MN}{8MN})^{-3} + 1 = \frac{3}{2} + 1 = \frac{5}{2} $$   which completes proof.

stem_md:
Is there a positive integer  $n$  for which the following holds: 
for an arbitrary rational  $r$  there exists an integer  $b$  and non-zero integers  $a _1, a_2, ..., a_n$  such that  $r=b+\frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+...+\frac{1}{a_n}$  ?
solution_md:
Such integer does not exist. For any and  $n\in\mathbb{N}$  we denote 
	  $$ S(n,t):=\left\{ \frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+\dots+\frac{1}{a_n}\le t: a_i\in\mathbb{N}, i=1,2,\dots,n \right\} $$   
	We prove the following claim.
	
	**Claim**. There exists  $\varepsilon >0$  (depending on  $n,t$ ) such that
	  $$ S(n,t)\cap (t-\varepsilon,t ]=\left\{ t-\varepsilon<\frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+\dots+\frac{1}{a_n}\le t: a_i\in\mathbb{N}, a_i\le N, i=1,2,\dots,n \right\} $$  	where  $N$  is some sufficiently large natural number.
	**Proof**. Induction on  $n$ . The claim holds for  $n=1$ . Suppose it holds for  $n-1$ . Let  $r\in S(n,t), t/2<r\le t$  and  $r=\frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+\dots+\frac{1}{a_n}$ . Then  $a_i\le \frac{2n}{t}$  for some  $1\le i\le n$ . WLOG suppose  $a_n\le \frac{2n}{t}$ . Thus, there are only finitely many options for  $a_n$ . Hence
	  $$ S(n,t)\cap (t/2,t]= \bigcup_{a=1}^{\lfloor 2n/t\rfloor}\left(\frac{1}{a}+\left\{\frac{t}{2}-\frac{1}{a}< \frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+\dots+\frac{1}{a_n}\le t-\frac{1}{a}: a_i\in\mathbb{N}, i=1,2,\dots,n \right\}\right) $$   
	  $$ S(n,t)\cap (t/2,t] = \bigcup_{a=1}^{\lfloor 2n/t\rfloor} \left(\frac{1}{a}+S(n-1, t-1/a)\cap (t/2,t]\right) $$  	For each  $a\in \mathbb{N}, 1\le a\le  2n/t$  there exists  $\varepsilon_a>0$  such that 
	\begin{align*}
	&\left(\frac{1}{a}+S(n-1,t-1/a)\right)\bigcap\left(t-\varepsilon_a,t\right]=
	&=\frac{1}{a}+\left\{t-\frac{1}{a}-\varepsilon_a< \frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+\dots+\frac{1}{a_{n-1}}\le t-\frac{1}{a}: a_i\in\mathbb{N}, a_i\le N_a, i=1,2,\dots,n-1 \right\} 
	\end{align*}
	Finally, it remains to take  $\varepsilon:=\min\{\varepsilon_a, a=1,2,\dots,\lfloor 2n/t\rfloor\}$  and  $N:=\max\{N_a, \lfloor 2n/t\rfloor\}:a=1,2,\dots,\lfloor 2n/t\rfloor$  to complete the induction step.  $\blacksquare$ 	
	Now, back to the OP. By the proven claim, for any  $n\in \mathbb{N}$  there exists  $\varepsilon>0$  and  $N>0$  such that
	  $$ S(n,1)\cap(1-\varepsilon,1]=\left\{ 1-\varepsilon<\frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+\dots+\frac{1}{a_n}\le 1: a_i\in\mathbb{N}, a_i\le N, i=1,2,\dots,n \right\} $$   
	But it is not possible the LHS to consists of all rationals in  $(1-\varepsilon,1]$  since the rationals  $\frac{k}{p}, k<p, p>N, p \text{ is a prime},$  are not present in the RHS for sufficiently large  $p$ .

Here's a solution motivated, in part, by #2.

Let  $S_n$  denote the set of rational numbers that can be written as  $b+\frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+\cdots + \frac{1}{a_n}$  for some integer  $b$  and non-zero  $a_1,a_2,\dotsc ,a_n$ . We claim that for every irrational number  $q$  and positive integer  $n$ , there exists a positive real number  $\epsilon_{q,n}$  such that  $s\not\in S_n$  for all  $s\in (q-\epsilon_{q,n},q+\epsilon_{q,n})$ . Note that since  $\mathbb{Q}$  is dense, this proposition yields the negative answer to the problem.

We will use induction on  $n$ . The base case  $n=1$  is rather obvious. Now, suppose we want to prove the case  $n=t+1$ . 
Consider an irrational number  $q$  and the interval  $$ I=\left( q-\frac{\epsilon_{q,t}}{2},q+\frac{\epsilon_{q,t}}{2}\right). $$  For any  $s\in I\cap S_{n+1}$ , we have  $s=b+\frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{1}{a_2}+\cdots + \frac{1}{a_n}+\frac{1}{a_{n+1}}$  for some choices of  $b,a_1,a_2,\dotsc ,a_{n+1}$ . 
By inductive hypothesis,  $$ s-\frac{1}{a_{n+1}}\not\in  (q-\epsilon_{q,t},q+\epsilon_{q,t})\implies \left| \frac{1}{a_{n+1}}\right|\geqslant \frac{\epsilon_{q,t}}{2}\implies a_{n+1}\in \{ -N,\dotsc ,-1,1,\dotsc, N\} $$  where  $N=\lfloor 2/\epsilon_{q,t}\rfloor$ . The same holds for  $a_1,a_2,\dotsc ,a_n$ . 
So, the set of fractional part of  $s$  for every  $s\in I\cap S_{n+1}$  is finite. 
We can deduce easily that there exists a sub-interval of  $I$  that does the job of the inductive step.

stem_md: The circle  $ \omega $  inscribed in triangle  $ABC$  touches its sides  $AB, BC, CA$  at points  $K, L, M$  respectively. In the arc  $KL$  of the circle  $ \omega $  that does not contain the point  $M$ , we select point  $S$ . Denote by  $P, Q, R, T$  the intersection points of straight  $AS$  and  $KM, ML$  and  $SC, LP$  and  $KQ, AQ$  and  $PC$  respectively. It turned out that the points  $R, S$  and  $M$  are collinear. Prove that the point  $T$  also lies on the line  $SM$ .
solution_md: Let  $SM \cap KL=Z$ . Note that, by Steiner's RatioTheorem, we have   $$ \frac{KP}{PM}=\frac{KS^2}{SM^2} \text{ AND } \frac{LQ}{QM}=\frac{LS^2}{SM^2} $$  Applying Ceva Theorem to  $\triangle KLM$ , we get   $$ \frac{KP}{PM} \times \frac{MQ}{QL} \times \frac{LZ}{KZ}=1 \Rightarrow \frac{KZ}{LZ}=\frac{KS^2}{LS^2} $$  Then Steiner's Ratio Theorem again gives us that  $SZ$  is the  $S$ -symmedian of  $\triangle SKL$ , or in other words,  $B \in SM$ . Now, denote  $U=AS \cap \omega$  and  $V=CS \cap \omega$ . Then we have   $$ (S,V;C,Q)=-1=(S,U;P,A) \stackrel{T}{=} (S,TU \cap SC;C,Q) \Rightarrow T \in UV $$  Also, taking  $X$  as  $SS \cap MM$  (tangents taken wrt  $\omega$ ), we have   $$ -1=(S,M;K,L)=(SS,MM;KK,LL)=(X,M;A,C) \stackrel{S}{=} (S,M;U,V) $$  So  $X \in UV$ . But then   $$ (X,M;A,C)=-1=(U,S;A,P) \stackrel{T}{=} (X,TS \cap AC;A,C) \Rightarrow T \in SM \quad \blacksquare $$

stem_md: Inside the inscribed quadrilateral  $ ABCD $ , a point  $ P $  is marked such that  $ \angle PBC = \angle PDA $ ,  $ \angle PCB = \angle PAD $ . Prove that there exists a circle that touches the straight lines  $ AB $  and  $ CD $ , as well as the circles circumscribed by the triangles  $ ABP $  and  $ CDP $ .
solution_md:
Define  $E=AB\cap CD$ ,  $F=AC\cap BD$ ,  $\omega$  is the circumcircle of  $ABCD$ ,  $O$  is the center of  $\omega$ ,  $R$  is the length of radius of  $\omega$ , and  $\ell$  is the internal bisector of  $\angle AED$ . $\textbf{Lemma :}$  There exist a circle  $\Gamma$  which is orthogonal to  $\omega$  and tangent to both  $AB$  and  $CD$ . $\textit{Proof :}$  Note that it suffices to prove that there exists point  $Y$  on  $\ell$  such that  $YO^{2}=YE^2\cdot (\sin \frac{\angle AED}{2})^2 + R^2$ . To do this we'll use cartesian coordinate.
WLOG  $E=(0,0)$ ,  $\ell$  is line  $y=x$ , and  $O=(p,q)$ . For any point  $K=(k,k)$  on line  $\ell$ , we consider function  $f(K)=(k-p)^2+(k-q)^2-2k^{2}\cdot (\sin \frac{\angle AED}{2})^2-R^2$ .
It's easy to see that  $f(K)$  will become a continuous function (it is a polynomial). Furthermore we also have when  $K=E$ ,  $f(K) > 0$  and when  $K\in \omega$ ,  $f(K) < 0$ . Thus by Intermediate Value Theorem, there exist  $K$  such that  $f(K)=0$ .
This implies  $KO^{2}=KE^{2}\cdot (\sin \frac{\angle AED}{2})^2 + R^2$  and the lemma is now proved.

Now define  $\Gamma$  as a circle which is orthogonal to  $\omega$  and tangent to both  $AB$  and  $CD$ . We'll prove that this circle is also tangent to both  $(ABP)$  and  $(CDP)$  which will finish this problem. By symmetry it suffices to prove  $\Gamma$  is tangent to  $(ABP)$ .

Note that  $\angle PBC=\angle PDA$  and  $\angle PCB=\angle PAD$  implies that  $P$  is the center of spiral similarity which sends  $DA$  to  $BC$ . Thus, we can get  $ADPF$  and  $BPCF$  are both cyclic.
After that, by simple angle chasing we can get  $ABPO$  and  $CDPO$  are both cyclic.

Define  $M$  as the contact point of  $\Gamma$  and  $AB$ ,  $N$  as the intersection of segment  $MO$  with  $\omega$  and  $N'$  as the intersection of line  $MO$  with  $\Gamma$  where  $N'\neq M$ Notice that inversion around  $\Gamma$  sends  $N$  to  $M$ , hence  $ON\times OM=R^{2}$ . But as  $\Gamma$  is orthogonal to  $\omega$  we also have  $ON'\times OM=R^{2}$ , so we must have  $N=N'$ .

After that, to prove that  $\Gamma$  is tangent to  $(ABP)$  it suffices to prove that tangent of  $\Gamma$  at  $M$  is parallel to tangent  $(ABP)$  at  $O$  which is true. (because line  $AB$  is line tangent to  $(ABP)$  which pass through  $M$  and  $OA=OB$  implies tangent to  $(ABP)$  at  $O$  is parallel to  $AB$ )

Therefore,  $\Gamma$  is tangent to  $(ABP)$  and the problem is now solved.
